quote: Alignment is making that loop's behavior stay something humans can still correct.
note: Grammatical referent is now the deployed loop. The gloss still keeps one of the eight join exports (correction) as the meaning of alignment; LayeredAlignedDef needs all eight. Same narrowing in ch01.082.

quote: The optimizer that actually steers outcomes is often the whole deployed loop, not the weights alone.
note: Hedged. Lean has no object-selection step: every join predicate takes an opaque System argument chosen outside the spine (ch01.003).

quote: Before asking whether a system is aligned, locate that loop.
note: Central spine finding for Ch. 1. In Lean the object is the System argument A, fixed before any predicate is applied. Nothing relates A to the risk-determining process. A case can be valid for A and yield Safe A through MB11 while the risk sits in a larger A'. BoundaryAligned is opaque, and MB1 speaks about a Boundary record (leakage), with no map from System to Boundary. So the chapter's first step happens outside the spine. Candidate 2.0 item: a relation between the evaluated system and the risk system, or a declared-setting argument carrying the risk (principle 3 context T).

quote: restates and extends observations already made in the embedded-agency, multi-agent-systems, and structural-AI-failure literature \autocite{demski2019embedded,christiano2019failure}.
note: Embedded agency now cited (demski2019embedded).

quote: This chapter adds a boundary-error typology and treats
note: The typology is the chapter's claimed addition; see ch01.037 for whether it partitions.

sec: The Standard Picture and Its Failure
quote: Any account of alignment fixes three things, usually without saying so
form: forall account. Fixes(account, object, subject, content)
note: Reading aid (stated as such two sentences later). Lean has the object slot (System) and the content slot (AlignmentTarget P); the subject slot (who aligns) has no term.

sec: The Standard Picture and Its Failure
quote: the first slot is often filled wrongly for capable deployed systems
form: forall A in CapableDeployed. ObjectSlot_standard(A) != RiskSystem(A)
note: Hedged to match 'often' in the thesis box and the exceptions in ch01.042.

sec: The Standard Picture and Its Failure
quote: once the object is misidentified, no choice of subject or content repairs the safety case
form: Misidentified(object) -> forall s c. not Repairs(s, c, Case)
note: The shape matches the conjunctive join: if BoundaryAligned fails, LayeredAlignedDef fails whatever the other conjuncts. But misidentification is not not-BoundaryAligned(A). It is a valid case about the wrong A. Lean cannot state that (ch01.003). The universal 'no choice' is argued only by example.

sec: The Standard Picture and Its Failure
quote: That picture is useful for toy domains, e.g., chess engines or robot vacuums, but it breaks for superintelligence.
form: Useful(StandardPicture, {chess, recommenders, vacuums}) and not Holds(StandardPicture, ASI)
note: Recommenders dropped from the toy list; they remain the later counterexample. UNHEDGED remains on 'breaks for superintelligence'.

sec: The Standard Picture and Its Failure
quote: the real agent may not be the model we train
note: Hedged possibility; the chapter's examples support it.

sec: The Standard Picture and Its Failure
quote: Human values are not a fixed or even always well-defined object.
form: not Fixed(HumanValues) and not always WellDefined(HumanValues)
note: Content-slot claim, asserted here and argued in Ch. 4. A forward reference would tell the reader where.

sec: The Standard Picture and Its Failure
quote: What we need is not a snapshot of today's labels but a dynamical condition
form: Needs(Alignment, DynamicalCondition) and not Needs(Alignment, Snapshot(labels))
note: Ch. 3 carries it; P01 is the basin-invariant shape.

quote: at which boundary, under which selection pressure, across which transformation, and through which correction channel
form: Aligned(with P, at B, under Sel, across T, via CC)
note: Good preview of the four spines: 'with what' is the content P, then boundary, selection, transformation (successor and transport) and correction. Grounding and adversarial robustness are absent; fine for Ch. 1.

quote: Those later questions presuppose that we have identified the relevant process.
form: forall q in LaterQuestions. Presupposes(q, Identified(Process))
note: In Lean the presupposition is built into typing (every predicate takes A : System), so it is satisfied vacuously, never checked. The warrant for the chapter's 'first question' rests on this record.

quote: Many alignment arguments begin too late.
note: Generalization over the field. The five questions that follow name agendas (corrigibility, deception, mesa-optimization) without citing them.

quote: They ask whether a trained network contains a mesa-optimizer \autocite{hubinger2019risks}.
note: Mesa-optimizer question now cited. Corrigibility and deception questions still have none.

quote: These are important questions.
note: Fragment repaired. Scene-setting; the load-bearing assumption is ch01.018.

quote: But they assume that we already know what object is being aligned.
form: forall q in FieldQuestions. Assumes(q, Known(Object))
note: Restates ch01.014. Both are needed by the reader, but the warrant is one premise.

quote: yet several of the others shape the effective optimization more than the weights do
form: exists k>=2 components c != Weights. Influence(c, EffOpt) > Influence(Weights, EffOpt)
note: No measure of 'shape the effective optimization more' and no evidence. A forward pointer to the measure that would decide it (predictive or control contribution, Ch. 7 or Ch. 11) would turn the claim into a checkable one.

quote: If we align the wrong object, we can get local success and global failure.
note: Correctly hedged; the four examples that follow show possibility.

quote: is the failure mode Christiano describes, in which no single model is obviously the thing to align
form: Describes(christiano2019failure, AggregateDrift and not exists m. Obviously(AlignTarget(m)))
note: A gloss, not Christiano's wording (his frame is proxy optimization and influence-seeking patterns). Not checked against the source in this pass.

quote: A regulator can certify model behavior while the real risk sits in how millions of users adapt to the system
note: One of four possibility examples. Decision-relevant for policy readers.

quote: The first alignment question is therefore:
note: Warrant chain is ch01.014 (restated in ch01.018) plus ch01.020. Valid as priority-of-question; it does not need that the model is usually wrong.

quote: Which subset of the world, if modeled as a bounded process with internal state, interface channels, and control capacity, best predicts the future changes we care about?
form: Q_where := argmax_{C subset World} PredFit(BoundedModel(C), Futures_cared)
note: First of several statements of the selection criterion: this one (best predicts, no cost term), the candidate definition (ch01.029, helps predict), the loop criterion (ch01.034), the prose cost comparison (ch01.044), the key-claim argmax (ch01.087), and Ch. 7's J(C). Lean has the interface part (EpsilonBoundary) and an MDL ordering over Model (S07), but no selection over candidate boundaries.

quote: the baby's brain arguably has to model a world where the acting entity is largely the composite unit of baby and caregiver.
form: forall infant, age < 18mo. Models(brain, ActingEntity = Composite(infant, caregiver))

strength.q: at least until about; arguably; largely

note: Hedged to match the preceding 'arguably'. Specific age still uncited; Ch. 9 carries the socialization cites.

quote: But the model alone does not contain the loop.
note: True by construction of the example.

quote: The composite can still optimize.
form: possible((forall c in Components. not Malicious(c)) and Optimizes(Composite))
note: The core possibility claim. 'Optimize' is not yet operational here; the control/compression condition (ch01.064) supplies it.

quote: In each case, the dangerous object may not be a model but a coupled adaptive loop.
form: forall d in Domains. possible(DangerObject(d) = AdaptiveLoop)
note: Generalizes one toy to eight domains, correctly hedged.

sec: Operational Definition of the Alignment Object
quote: A candidate is a subset of the world whose interface helps predict the outcomes we care about.
form: Candidate(C) := C subset World and HelpsPredict(Interface(C), Outcomes_cared)
note: Lean defines AgentCandidate b := BoundaryCondition b (screening at the interface). The prose candidate is defined by predictive help. These are different criteria. Ch. 7's J(C) needs both (residual and predictive term). Either definition alone admits what the other excludes: a sealed rock passes screening, and a leaky but predictive cluster passes predictive help.

sec: Operational Definition of the Alignment Object
quote: The point is to make the attribution pay rent.
form: Attribute(Agent, C) only if Improves(Prediction or Decision)
note: Plain statement of the MDL penalty that comes later.

sec: Operational Definition of the Alignment Object
quote: an information cut at the interface, a memory-localization handle, and a compression test for goal-like modeling
note: Now three tests, matching Boundary Discovery (ch01.062 to ch01.064) and the Summary (ch01.092). ROOT-VARIANTS remains vs the candidate definition (ch01.029). The membrane contrast is a footnote on ch01.032, not a second definition in the body.

quote: the boundary that matters is wherever the control loop runs.
note: Body stays with physical examples. Membrane language and the information-theoretic cut are a footnote pointing at Ch. 7.

quote: Physical containment is evidence.
note: Hedged with the next sentence.

quote: The relevant question is whether there is a persistent transformation from input to internal update to output to future input.
form: Relevant(C) iff Persistent(Loop(in -> update -> out -> in'))
note: Yet another criterion: loop persistence. It maps most closely to the memory condition (ch01.063). 'Persistent' is undefined.

quote: It changes the world from which its next training distribution is drawn.
note: Standard performative-prediction point. perdomo2020 is in references/manuscript-citations.bib if a cite is wanted.

quote: A boundary error occurs when the system being evaluated or aligned is not among the bounded processes whose dynamics determine the relevant risk, or omits one of them when several matter at once.
form: BoundaryError(E, r) := Evaluated(E) != the C such that Determines(Dyn(C), r)
note: Named definition; no Lean predicate. Author 2026-10-16: Ch. 1 illustrates with one boundary; several allowed (ch01.058, ch01.066). Minimal Lean would relate evaluated System to risk process(es).

quote: Some misfits concern \emph{extent}: the chosen boundary is too narrow or too wide relative to the process that drives the risk.
note: Typology contribution: extent (narrow, wide, misplaced in Ch. 7) vs resolution (timescale, abstraction). Not claimed as a complete partition; 'several forms' is intentional.

quote: This is probably the most common technical version: evaluators usually score the model.
note: Hedged. Still no citation of evaluation practice; the hedge carries the claim.

quote: The risk is that the composition creates a new control loop.
note: Mechanism statement, fine.

quote: A useful boundary must support prediction, intervention, and measurement.
form: Useful(C) -> Supports(C, prediction) and Supports(C, intervention) and Supports(C, measurement)
note: Consistent with the key claim (ch01.087) (predictive relevance, intervention-relevant constraint); measurement is implicit there.

quote: It is a property of a trajectory.
form: Aligned : Trajectory -> Prop, not State -> Prop
note: Join predicates and Safe take a System, not a trajectory. Time enters the spine only through basin invariants (P01, P35) and successor chains. The 2.0 parameterization does not add time either. Note it alongside the D, T and setting arguments.

sec: When the Model Is the Right Object
quote: Sometimes the model is the right object.
form: exists A. ObjectSlot(A) = Model(A) is correct
note: Falsifiability guard, and it is what readers will trust. It conflicts with the flat universal ch01.007.

sec: When the Model Is the Right Object
quote: The test is whether the larger boundary improves prediction of the relevant failure modes enough to justify the added complexity.
form: Prefer(C2 over C1) iff DeltaPred(C2, C1 | failure modes) > lambda * DeltaComplexity(C2, C1)
note: S07 (Gain > 0 -> Preferred) is the same shape but orders Model, not boundaries. The Boundary record in Lean carries only leakage and a blanket witness: no predictive or description-length field.

sec: When the Model Is the Right Object
quote: The composite must explain more than it costs.
note: Prose comparison only. The displayed pairwise inequality is not in Ch. 7; Ch. 7 states J(C) = R - alpha P + lambda Omega. ROOT-VARIANTS remains vs the key-claim prose (ch01.087), which still drops the boundary residual.

sec: When the Model Is the Right Object
quote: Otherwise the framework becomes unfalsifiable.
note: Sound, and the strongest reader-trust sentence in the chapter.

quote: Once boundary errors matter, alignment becomes partly a measurement problem.
note: Hedged. MB1 is exactly the measurement-to-predicate step.

quote: Which human correction signals still causally affect future action?
note: The audit list covers boundary, memory, objectives, correction and successors. Grounding, bundle, bearer and adversarial items come later; fine for Ch. 1.

quote: These questions change deployment decisions.
note: Backed by the five conditionals that follow. This is the legibility hinge for funders.

quote: If the relevant boundary includes the product-feedback loop, then predeployment model evals are insufficient.
note: Clean trigger. The conditional form is the right hedge.

quote: If the relevant boundary includes market incentives, then procurement and liability become alignment mechanisms.
note: Policy-facing trigger.

quote: If the relevant boundary includes successor creation, then tool access and model-writing privileges become central risks.
note: Points at the successor box.

quote: If the relevant boundary includes the lab itself, then governance cannot be cleanly separated from technical alignment.
note: Funder-relevant; consistent with the selection box.

quote: We would ask whether harmed people can correct the system.
note: The subject slot shifts from developers to affected people. That is consistent with ch01.079 and is worth saying once explicitly, since the opening frame names developers as the subject.

quote: The fact that the bureaucracy is not conscious does not make it non-agentic for safety purposes.
form: not Conscious(B) does not imply not Agentic_safety(B)
note: The anti-anthropomorphism hinge; scoped by 'for safety purposes'.

quote: Those are enough to matter.
form: Memory and Interface and Selection and SelfPreservingRoutines -> SafetyRelevantAgent
note: The sufficiency set differs from the three discovery conditions (ch01.062 to ch01.064) (boundary, memory, control/compression): 'selection' and 'self-preserving routines' replace the control condition. Either name the mapping or reuse the three conditions.

quote: The real optimizer may be any stable subset of this list.
form: forall S subset List. Stable(S) -> possible(RealOptimizer = S)
note: 'Stable' undefined (the persistence of ch01.034, or the boundary condition ch01.062?).

quote: Or several at once.
note: Several optimizers at once; consistent with ch01.036 (omit when several matter) and ranked output ch01.066. Single-risk argmax in ch01.087 is one operationalization.

quote: This creates a hierarchy of candidate boundaries:
form: scale-order(C_weights, C_session, C_scaffold, C_product, C_company, C_industry-state); relation is a DAG, not a tree
note: Hierarchy of scale kept. Footnote: not a tree; a company does not include its customers; one part can sit in several larger candidates; the relation is a DAG. The subset signs order scale.

quote: Alignment at one level can be defeated by selection at another.
note: Preview of the selection box (Ch. 34, MB6).

quote: The correct answer may vary by risk.
note: Risk-relativity carries into the key claim (ch01.087) ('for the risk in question'). BoundaryAligned is not risk-indexed. Under principle 3 the threat model T is a context parameter fixed per case, so one case gets one boundary. Ch. 1 implies one boundary per risk inside a case.

quote: Knowing what crosses that interface is enough to predict how the inside and the outside affect each other.
note: Prose preview of the epsilon-boundary. The mutual-information formula is in Ch. 7, not here. MB1 still bridges a measured certificate to BoundaryCondition.

quote: The candidate stores something that still matters later.
note: Prose memory handle: stored state still predicts the next step after the current interface is known. The mutual-information form is in Ch. 7. Lean has no memory predicate (MemoryLineage is a successor relation).

quote: What the candidate does is better predicted by saying what it is steering toward than by listing only its parts.
note: Prose control handle. If the goal adds no prediction, do not attribute one. The description-length formula is in Ch. 22. Same shape as S07.

quote: They are measurement handles
note: Honest. It matches MB1 being a bridge, not a theorem.

quote: The practical output is a ranked list of candidate optimizers:
note: A posterior over candidates, while the three conditions are thresholds. How the ranking is computed is not stated. It fits ch01.058, not the single winner reading of ch01.087.

quote: A boundary card would describe the optimizer around the model.
note: The most quotable artifact in the chapter. It appears only here in the manuscript; a site card or later-chapter pickup would give it conductivity.

quote: Passive observation is weak.
note: Lean supports it: P09 (observationally equivalent models with different goals means the goal is not identifiable) and P36 (a distinguishing handle operation refines identification). Both are short definitional proofs; confirm with #print axioms before citing. Ch. 1 could name the result in one clause.

quote: The question is whether the same latent control structure reappears.
form: AgencyTest(C) := forall p in Perturbations. LatentControl(C after p) ~ LatentControl(C)
note: Operational test; Ch. 39 develops it.

quote: The red flag is control-locus continuity under changed surface conditions.
form: RedFlag := SurfaceChanged and RationaleChanged and Persists(InferredControlObjective)
note: Lean's ControlLocusPreserved is the seventh successor conserved property (Ch. 31 and Ch. 48). Here the same idea is a perturbation red flag. The concept is introduced here and then omitted from this chapter's own list of preserved properties (ch01.075).

quote: Under those conditions, the real boundary may move.
note: Hedged; warrant is the preceding capability list.

quote: The alignment object is therefore not a fixed object.
note: Object-slot wording. Lean AlignmentTarget remains the content slot; this sentence no longer collides with it. Equivalence-class transitivity is still an author decision (ch01.073).

quote: It is a chain of admissible transitions: each step must preserve the correction-relevant invariants below, not membership in one fixed snapshot.
form: AlignmentObject := chain C_0 -> C_1 -> ... with Admissible(T_i, invariants)
note: Author: chain of admissible transitions, not an equivalence class (~ not transitive under drift). Aligns with SuccessorSafe as step relation.

quote: We need to ask whether each transformation preserves those invariants:
note: Matches the step relation SuccessorSafe A B.

quote: \item control-locus continuity.
form: ~ := BoundaryClosure and MemoryLineage and BundleGeometry and BearerMaps and CCCapacity and TransparencyPolicy and SuccessorConstraints
note: Seventh item now matches Ch. 31 and Lean ControlLocusPreserved. CCIPreserved vs 'correction-channel capacity' remains a Ch. 31 gap, not Ch. 1's.

quote: A claim is useful only if it changes decisions.
note: Now the necessity reading, matching ch42.010.

quote: Do not log only prompts and outputs.
form: Must(Log(tool calls, memory writes, gates, user adaptation, metrics, finetune inputs, deploy decisions, institutional feedback))
note: Concrete and operational. Warrant: the data for the boundary conditions sits outside the model trace (next sentence).

quote: Sometimes the safest model-level change is less important than changing the surrounding selection pressure.
note: Hedged; previews the selection box.

quote: They observe different parts of the boundary.
form: forall r in Roles. Observes(r, Part_r(Boundary)) and Part_r differ
note: Warrant for the inclusion list; widens the subject slot (ch01.054).

quote: Failure includes hidden boundary expansion, correction-channel erosion, goal laundering, successor creation without invariant preservation, and selection for opacity.
form: Failure contains {HiddenBoundaryExpansion, CCErosion, GoalLaundering, SuccessorWithoutInvariants, SelectionForOpacity}
note: Maps onto the boundary, correction, successor and selection boxes plus Ch. 40. 'Includes' marks it non-exhaustive; good.

quote: bounded optimizer
note: The table fixes 'bounded optimizer', but the chapter names the object as candidate, real optimizer, real agent, bounded process, adaptive loop, control locus and alignment target. The substitution table is the natural place to say which of these are the same object.

quote: preserved correction relation
note: Consistent with the thesis gloss (ch01.001), with the same narrowing to the correction export.

quote: Mitigation requires held-out prediction, perturbation, and simplicity penalties.
form: Mitigate(SpuriousClusters) -> HeldOut and Perturbation and SimplicityPenalty
note: Ties back to the MDL rule.

quote: A system selected to pass boundary audits may distribute its control traces.
note: The boundary audit is itself a steerable channel. In Lean, MB1 (epsilon-certificate -> BoundaryCondition) has no AdversariallyVerifiableUpTo antecedent. The G0 gate discussion in Ch. 42 names only MB6b, MB7b and MB7c. Camouflage of the boundary estimator would belong there too. Candidate addition to the G2 restatement list.

quote: It is not sufficient.
form: Necessary(FindOptimizer, Alignment) and not Sufficient(FindOptimizer, Alignment)
note: Matches Lean: BoundaryAligned is one conjunct of LayeredAlignedDef, so it is necessary and not sufficient.

quote: Before aligning anything, locate the bounded processes whose dynamics matter for the risk in question.
note: Restates locate-first thesis; plural processes matches ch01.036.

quote: The key claim states what locating means operationally: among boundaries that are intervention-relevant for the risk in question, the alignment object is the one whose predictive relevance most exceeds its description cost---the candidate that best trades forecast power for parsimony.
note: Operational key claim (selection rule). Thesis ordering: ch01.003, ch01.687. ROOT-VARIANTS vs Ch. 7 J(C) intentional; ranked list ch01.066 for several optimizers.

quote: This makes optimizing the wrong thing less likely, and more detectable.
note: Hedged to match the Limits section (overfitting, hidden common causes, adversarial camouflage).

quote: the composite never acquires surplus
form: Refutes(ch01) if forall transitions. not Acquires(Composite, Surplus) and Suffices(AlignVisibleModel)
note: 'Surplus' is Ch. 43's affordable surplus (cost of faking) and is undefined in Ch. 1. The falsifier itself is empirical and fair.

quote: Reliable steering is control, so an effective agent exists by construction
form: ReliableSteering -> exists EffectiveAgent; Refutes(ch01) only if Proof(not Localizable-before-action(DecisiveController))
note: Formal falsifier bar (proof of non-localizability). Empirical counterpart: ch01.094.

quote: Alignment arguments often begin too late because they assume the alignment object is already known.
note: Uses 'alignment object', the right term; contrast ch01.093.

quote: Boundary discovery uses interface screening, memory localization, and intentional compression as measurement handles.
note: Three handles, matching Boundary Discovery; ch01.031 lists two.

quote: For superintelligence, the alignment object may be a chain of admissible transitions, not a fixed snapshot.
note: Matches ch01.073; object-slot wording.

quote: Repeated high-stakes incidents in which investigation still cannot identify which bounded process steered the outcome---despite traces, tools, and institutional records of the kind this chapter recommends---or in which the decisive controller becomes clear only after harm.
note: Empirical WWCTV added 2026-10-16; pairs with proof bar in ch01.090.
